stories.title: How Intentful uses dots to make more time for growth
stories.summary: Marina Petrova’s dot Aria helps research websites and build proposals, while proactively flagging messages and resolving issues.

sources.name: OpenAI
sources.title: How Intentful uses dots to make more time for growth
sources.text: How a small business founder’s dot helps her with research and proposals, while alerting her to critical messages and resolving issues. Marina Petrova is CEO and cofounder of Intentful ⁠ (opens in a new window) , a lean team that helps brands make their marketing interactive, with products such as ads that answer customers’ questions in real time and tools that make website information readable by AI. The company also advises and trains marketers on using AI. In travel and tourism, Intentful works with destination organizations and local businesses such as hotels, restaurants, and attractions. A custom proposal is part of how Marina wins their business, showing prospects what’s possible and what it would take to deliver. To keep Intentful growing, she needed more room for that strategic work, but she was spending too much time on research, hunting for files, and formatting decks. Her dot ⁠ changed all that, taking on tasks and meeting Marina’s needs before she even had to ask. For one of Intentful’s tourism clients, Marina wanted to propose a package of Intentful’s AI services for hundreds of local businesses in the destination. Before she could price the package, she needed to work out which businesses’ websites the package could cover and what Intentful had charged other clients for similar work. She brought in her dot, which she named Aria, to help her get from research to a proposal she could put her name on in a few hours instead of several days. First, Marina gave Aria a spreadsheet of URLs and criteria for deciding which sites to include. For example, a site needed a readable sitemap listing no more than 3,000 pages. Next, Aria helped Marina research pricing. Through ChatGPT ⁠ (opens in a new window) plugins, Aria reviewed Intentful’s sales data, including past engagements and discussions in HubSpot. It surfaced pricing from earlier agreements and context from Intentful’s plans for the following year. Using that data, Marina and Aria then built a pricing model: page counts determined the pricing tier, and previous customer agreements also informed the price. “We worked through a custom pricing model together, and then Aria turned it into a one-page proposal I reviewed and edited,” said Marina. When drafting proposals, Aria knows to use Intentful’s templates from Google Drive. Marina can also point Aria to an earlier proposal as a reference, so the draft follows Intentful’s style from the start. “I need to say what needs to be in a proposal, but I don’t need to spend an hour figuring out its layout. My dot handles that,” Marina says. Aria can also spot things Marina hadn’t thought to check. When Marina asked Aria to reuse pricing from an earlier proposal, it noticed that the original renewal date didn’t match the timing she remembered. Aria flagged the discrepancy and left the date out of the new draft. Marina uses the Gmail and Slack plugins in ChatGPT to catch up on conversations, find open tasks, and see where the team needs her. Aria checks for messages that need Marina’s attention. While Marina was offline, Aria spotted a reply she had been waiting for and let her know it included an invitation for a call that morning. Marina also uses Aria to talk through ideas, find conversations, check an account’s history in the CRM, or open and assign tasks in Asana. She often briefs Aria by phone while she travels. Marina loves that her dot works in the tools she already uses. When Aria writes a draft, Marina can leave comments in Google Docs exactly where she wants changes. On longer documents, she asks Aria to use suggesting mode so she can see what changed. Aria also keeps up with changes in shared work without being asked. For a conference presentation, Marina created the deck and a colleague added two slides. “Aria noticed the new slides, updated the speaker notes without being asked, and let me know,” Marina says. Marina chooses which information Aria can access and always reviews outgoing email. She can keep work moving without handing over the final call. When Marina prepared an AI 101 session on agents, she used Aria to help build the lesson. The process was itself an example of what she wanted attendees to learn: delegate a real task, give the agent enough context, challenge the result, and stay in control of what goes out. Aria’s support continued even after the class. After a flight, Marina saw a participant’s request for access to a training file. When she checked with Aria, it had already shared the file. And after a session for 50 marketers, Aria noticed that a software glitch was preventing participants from opening the recording. It flagged the access issue and offered to fix it before the link was shared. Product updates, practical guides, upcoming events, and more.

stories.title: How iFood scales coding agents across 15,000 repositories

sources.name: OpenAI
sources.title: How iFood scales coding agents across 15,000 repositories
sources.text: as many vulnerabilities fixed through the security platform The Remote Agents Platform turned engineering tasks into API calls: teams delegate the work, execution takes place in a remote sandbox, and the result comes back as a merge request. In the internal security platform, the number of vulnerabilities fixed more than doubled. iFood maintains more than 15,000 code repositories. Each periodically needs specific tasks performed: validating code to ensure it meets internal standards, fixing vulnerable dependencies, or running an analysis. None of these tasks is difficult on its own. The challenge comes when those tasks multiply. “Solving this for one repository is easy. The challenge is solving it at scale,” says Victor Coelho, Senior Software Engineer at iFood. “The Remote Agents Platform is designed to make it possible to solve this at scale across all 15,000 repositories.” Before the platform, each team tackled the problem in its own way—and they all ran into the same obstacle. “Before, we had fragmented solutions. Imagine several teams at iFood trying to solve different problems, but without this layer, this agentic runtime, available to them. In the end, those solutions always ran into the same problem.” What was missing wasn’t intelligence or a use case. It was execution infrastructure. A dedicated runtime . The team describes the Remote Agents Platform as an API that launches a remote agentic coding task. The cycle has three steps: the user submits a prompt and environment requirements through a REST call; the platform processes the task on a dedicated remote runner inside an isolated sandbox; and the result is retrieved later. “The platform’s entry point, its interface, is a simple REST API. Users can use this API to create the runs they need. Internally, we handle and manage the entire lifecycle and delegate execution to isolated sandboxes,” he explains. Task progress can be monitored in real time. The runner’s internal design alternates between two different types of steps—and that combination makes the overall workflow predictable. Deterministic steps bookend the workflow: cloning the repository, importing the skills the agent can use, and setting up the working branch at the start; publishing the merge request and making the generated artifacts available at the end. In between is the agentic execution itself, running GPT‑5.6 Luna inside the sandbox. “It’s a combination of those two things: deterministic steps and agentic execution within the workflow.” The sandbox runs Ubuntu and includes the toolchains iFood’s ecosystem requires—Python, Java, Kotlin, C#, TypeScript, Rust, JavaScript, and Go—along with general-purpose tools. Beyond the sandbox, the agent can access Nexus, GitLab, Docker, Snyk, Kubernetes, and AWS. The model choice came down to three factors considered together, rather than just one. “We chose GPT‑5.6 Luna because, among models at the same checkpoint, the benchmarks showed it offered a great balance of intelligence, efficiency, and execution speed—how quickly it could complete tasks. Those three qualities together led us to choose GPT‑5.6 Luna.” That balance matters more for a platform built to scale than it would for a one-off use case. With tens of thousands of tokens being consumed, the average cost of four U.S. cents per run stops being a minor detail and becomes an architectural consideration. Delegating execution at scale creates a new challenge: automatically determining whether the agent did what it was supposed to do. iFood’s answer comes in the step after the session. Once execution is complete, the result is processed using OpenAI’s Structured Outputs, which requires the output to conform to a predefined contract. The platform already powers an internal iFood security product that scans the 15,000 repositories for vulnerable dependencies and attempts to fix them. The migration had a direct impact: “With our platform, the accuracy of those changes, those fixes, more than doubled,” says Coelho. This use case illustrates the idea behind the platform: the security team didn’t need to build its own agentic runtime or become experts in agent orchestration. It needed to call an API. The team emphasizes what asynchronous execution frees developers to do, rather than replacement. Because the task is delegated and runs without supervision, the developer doesn’t have to stay focused on monitoring it. “While they’re in a meeting, they can launch a code fix, a performance analysis, or another task that’s a little more routine—something they can delegate without having to monitor it at that moment.” Routine work no longer competes for the team’s attention. That leaves time for problems that require judgment. The Remote Agents Platform was designed as an internal layer with similarities to the way OpenAI makes this type of task available to external customers. “The Remote Agents Platform drew a lot of inspiration from OpenAI’s APIs, both the Batch API and the Agents API, which is an even more recent OpenAI product. We built a platform that resembles those products, but is internal to iFood.” The inspiration went beyond the concept. It extends to the design of the interfaces, the organization of resources, and the approach to asynchronous execution with results retrieved later. The platform has completed more than 25,000 tasks, consuming more than 27 billion tokens, at an average cost of US$0.04 per run. After migrating to the Remote Agents Platform, the internal security platform more than doubled both the accuracy of its fixes and the number of vulnerabilities resolved. Coverage extends across iFood’s more than 15,000 code repositories. All runs use GPT‑5.6 Luna, chosen for its balance of intelligence, efficiency, and speed. Structured Outputs ensures that each session returns a result that follows a predefined contract, whether positive or negative. stories.title: Clay helps sales teams win with Codex and ChatGPT
stories.summary: ChatGPT and Codex integrations help Clay’s users research deals and turn data into go-to-market plays, with GPT-6 models handling the reasoning.

sources.name: OpenAI
sources.title: Clay helps sales teams win with Codex and ChatGPT
sources.text: ChatGPT and Codex integrations help Clay users research deals and turn data into go-to-market plays, and GPT‑6 models handle the reasoning. Even when sales teams have plenty of data about a prospect, they can still struggle to understand what matters most and develop a winning pitch. Clay ⁠ (opens in a new window) is a self-learning revenue engine designed to help. Using GPT‑6 Astra, GPT‑6 Sol, and other models, Clay enables users to build lists of companies and people, enrich those records using agents, and use that information in go-to-market plays. Clay also brings these capabilities to where customers are already working with plugins for Codex and ChatGPT, making it easier to create and run go-to-market workflows and research accounts and deals. “Clay in ChatGPT gives sales reps a way to understand more about the customers they’re trying to sell to. It brings all of that rich context to the places they’re already working.” Clay’s Codex integration lets builders create and run go-to-market plays in Codex, while giving sales reps access to data they can use to research an account or understand a deal they’re trying to close. Jeff has seen reps combine information from their own systems and public datasets to determine how to best communicate their product’s value to a customer. “Customers love using Codex for a lot of different tasks in sales,” he says. “We’ve seen the best sales reps be the most empowered by this.” Clay’s ChatGPT plugin brings the same customer data into another tool reps already use, helping them learn more about prospects without leaving ChatGPT. Jeff says, “It’s been a big success.” OpenAI models power Claygent’s research, qualification, enrichment, and signal detection, as well as the agent that helps users build workflows and coordinate other Clay agents. Clay uses GPT‑6 Sol as its primary model, with GPT‑6 Astra for harder tasks and GPT‑6 Luna for cost-sensitive work. That range supports background research and copywriting as well as agents that users work with directly. The Responses API lets Clay use different levels of intelligence and cost through the same interface. “Having the same Responses API across the different price points is something that’s super appealing to us with OpenAI models,” said Jeff. GPT‑6 Astra also helps Jeff build and test software. He used to spend much of his time manually checking features he had built; now he can ask GPT‑6 Astra to handle more of that work. He explains, “GPT‑6 Astra really changed how I build software because it fully closed the loop on the engineering process. Now I can have Astra write code, add tests, and then actually run the tests and test the feature and record that and upload that in the PR. It simplifies my life a lot.” For Clay’s customers, Jeff sees GPT‑Live‑1 as a way to use Clay and Codex by voice and help prospects learn about a product. Clay is working on inbound sales development features that would let an agent show a product or service to a prospect. He also sees the Decisions API as another way to integrate models into Clay and open up new use cases. Clay’s ambition is to carry go-to-market workflows from start to finish, with agents that improve as they learn from the results. For Jeff, the goal is to empower builders “to bring the same shift that happened in software engineering to go-to-market.” Product updates, practical guides, upcoming events, and more.

stories.title: Introducing preemptible compute: the same compute, half the price
stories.summary: Together GPU Clusters now supports preemptible compute: the same GPU capacity at a flat 50% of the on-demand rate, with a five-minute drain window.

sources.name: Together AI
sources.title: Introducing preemptible compute: the same compute, half the price
sources.text: Preemptible compute is now generally available on Together GPU Clusters, on Kubernetes and Slurm clusters in all regions. Preemptible nodes give teams a lower-cost way to run interruption-tolerant work — short experiments, inference bursts, batch jobs — on the same GPU infrastructure they already use, billed sub-hourly at a flat 50% of the on-demand rate. You can add preemptible capacity to a new or existing cluster starting today. Preemptible compute adds a second compute type to Together GPU Clusters. Standard nodes are fulfilled synchronously and are never preempted. Preemptible nodes use the same NVIDIA accelerated compute, draw from un-used capacity, and can be reclaimed when that capacity is needed elsewhere. Preemptible nodes are billed at a flat 50% of the on-demand rate. The rate remains fixed rather than moving with a spot market. When a node is reclaimed, the cluster follows a five-minute drain (maximum 5 minutes) sequence: The cluster retains its preemptible target after the node is removed and automatically refills toward that target as capacity becomes available. You do not need to request replacement capacity. Billing is sub-hourly, with usage metered every one to two minutes. A node that runs for 12 minutes is billed for approximately 12 minutes. Preemptible nodes are not a separate cluster type. They join your existing cluster, labeled together.ai/compute-class=preemptible , so interruptible workers run on discounted capacity while coordinators, login pods, and serving replicas stay on standard nodes. The five-minute reclamation sequence makes recovery behavior the deciding factor. Work that can resume, retry, or requeue can use preemptible capacity while critical components should remain on standard nodes. Short experiments. Ablations, config sweeps, quick fine-tunes, evals, distillation, and batch inference are good candidates when the work can resume from a checkpoint or retry after a worker disappears. Frameworks such as Ray Train and PyTorch Lightning resume from the latest checkpoint without intervention. As a reference point, a full weight model checkpoint for GLM5.3 Flash, 321B parameter model is roughly 3.5TB which would take between 22s to 4mins to write to a parallel filesystem even at degraded performance. Leaving headroom inside the five-minute drain window. Temporary bursts. When batch or internal inference demand spikes, add cheaper preemptible nodes to absorb the burst and non-critical workloads instead of holding standard capacity sized for your peak or risking burst standard compute availability. Interrupted requests requeue; user-facing replicas remain on standard nodes. The common thread: work that is chunked, checkpointed, or retryable. Multi-day runs without checkpointing and strict-SLO serving with no fallback are not a fit. Together has a strong culture dogfooding , several internal research, dev/test and non-critical production workloads at Together are based on our preemptible compute based GPU clusters enabling us to leverage our spare capacity across product teams. After the workload is prepared for preemption, setup has two parts: set the preemptible target and schedule eligible work onto the labeled nodes. You can set the target when creating a cluster or on a cluster that is already running, using the Together Cloud console, CLI, or API. The API reports both the requested target, desired_preemptible_gpus , and the capacity currently live, allocated_preemptible_gpus . Because preemptible nodes draw from unused capacity, allocated capacity can remain below the desired target when capacity is tight. Choose your standard node count, then add a preemptible target on top. Scale up the preemptible target when you need additional worker capacity, then lower it when the work is complete. The cluster remains running throughout. Preemption notices are delivered as SIGTERM to the pod, as Kubernetes events ( reason=TogetherPreemptionNotified ), in the console's Event Timeline, and via the Together API's node_lifecycle_events — handling patterns are covered in the docs . Preemptible compute is generally available on Kubernetes and Slurm clusters.
